items.title: Meet Skore: Build reliable Tabular AI models faster
items.author: Probabl
items.content:
<article>Agents now build machine learning pipelines in seconds, a task that used to take a data science team a week or more.

But speed without methodology gives you black boxes: models you can’t explain, audit or reproduce. 

Enterprises shouldn’t have to choose between AI speed and confidence in the results. 

That’s why we built Skore, the platform for building reliable Tabular AI models faster. Keep your craft, your tools, and your judgment, without losing speed.

In this 1-minute demo, see how Skore helps data scientists build reliable tabular AI models faster, in 7 steps:

1️⃣ Connect to the Skore agent from your command line.

2️⃣ Plug in your preferred AI coding tool.

3️⃣ Connect the muscles of your AI coding tool with the brain of Skore.

4️⃣ Follow a guided workflow built for data science.

5️⃣ Switch the AI model to manage your token cost.

6️⃣ Audit how the agent runs multiple machine learning experiments.

7️⃣ See the best trade-off for your job, across accuracy, Brier score, log loss, ROC AUC, and prediction time.

Skore’s agent agent builds, validates, and tracks models and applies the statistical methodology of the scikit-learn maintainers at every step. The result: predictive models you can ship with confidence. 
🔗 Discover more about Skore: https://www.probabl.ai/skore/
Built by Probabl, the Tabular AI company founded by the creators and stewards of scikit-learn.</article>

items.title: scikit-learn version 1.9 highlights: GPU acceleration with the Python array API standard
items.author: Probabl
items.content:
<article>In this installment of our series on version 1.9, scikit-learn contributor Emily Chen explains how you can accelerate your scikit-learn workflows on GPUs.

For the past decade, scikit-learn has delegated computations to core dependencies like NumPy, SciPy, and Cython. All three were designed for CPUs, which meant that scikit-learn workflows were limited to CPUs, too. 

For  data science teams with access to GPUs, that design has become a bottleneck. GPU support promised significant speed-ups. But until recently, supporting GPUs meant writing a separate code path for every array library: one for NumPy, one for CuPy, another for PyTorch. For a project of scikit-learn's size, that meant fragmented code, a heavy maintenance burden, and a form of vendor lock-in that its maintainers were not willing to accept. 
 
💡The Python array API standard offers a solution. It is a shared specification for NumPy-like operations, adopted by the major array libraries. By writing to the standard rather than to a specific library, scikit-learn stays backend agnostic. Developers from Probabl, Quansight, NVIDIA, and the wider scientific community have been heads-down making GPU support an option in scikit-learn.</article>
